core: Every transaction keeps both sides equal
detail: Assets: what the business owns
Liabilities: what it owes outsiders
Owner's equity: owner's claim (assets minus liabilities)
Base of: double entry accounting and the balance sheet
Expanded: equity = capital + revenue minus expenses minus drawings
Doesn't balance → error
cards.formula: Assets = Liabilities + Owner's Equity
cards.example: Hodges and Sons balance sheet: assets $769,001 = liabilities $17,020 + owner's equity $751,981.
cards.say_it: Every transaction we record changes at least two items, but the equation always stays in balance, which is our first check that the books are right.
mistakes: Thinking one side can change alone; both sides change equally, or two items on one side move opposite

Cash purchase: credit Cash; credit purchase: credit Accounts Payable
n/30: full amount due in 30 days
2/10, n/30: 2% discount if paid in 10 days

cards.say_it: Because the customer will pay in 30 days, this is a credit sale, so I debit Accounts Receivable and still record the revenue today.

detail: Assets: owned, future benefit (cash, receivables, equipment, horses, land)
Liabilities: obligations (accounts payable, mortgage, line of credit)
Equity: owner's interest (capital, retained earnings), also statement of owner's equity
Revenue: earned selling goods or services; expenses: costs of earning it
Owner's withdrawals: reduce equity, not expenses
Classification decides: which statement, whether net income is affected
cards.example: New gym: Equipment, Cash and Accounts Receivable are assets; Accounts Payable is a liability; Owner's Capital is equity (all balance sheet); Salaries Expense is on the income statement. Edgewood Equestrian: boarding income is revenue, hay is an expense, the mortgage is a liability.
cards.say_it: Your trainers' salaries go on the income statement as an expense, but the treadmills are an asset on the balance sheet because they'll serve you for years.
mistakes: Treating owner's withdrawals as an expense, or forgetting to include any equity account

detail: Purpose: shows income statement activity reaching the balance sheet
Revenue: increases equity; expenses: decrease it
Net income (revenue minus expenses): flows into capital at closing
Owner investments: increase capital directly
Drawings: reduce capital directly, never an expense
cards.formula: Assets = Liabilities + Capital + Revenue minus Expenses minus Drawings
cards.example: Best Coffee: equity rises $100,000 + $50,000 of revenue and falls $23,500 of wage expense, for $126,500; assets $162,500 = liabilities $36,000 + equity $126,500.
cards.say_it: Revenue and expenses are really just temporary pieces of owner's equity, which is why net income ends up increasing your capital at year end.
mistakes: Treating drawings as an expense; they reduce equity but not net income

Equity: owner's claim (Capital, Drawings, Retained Earnings)

Expenses: costs used up to earn revenue (Wages, Rent, Utilities, Depreciation)
Balance sheet: assets, liabilities, equity
Income statement: revenue, expenses

cards.say_it: Horses are assets here because the ranch will use them for years to earn boarding and lesson revenue, while hay is an expense because it is used up quickly.
mistakes: Classifying a long-lived item as an expense or a monthly bill as an asset

Purchase: acquires goods or services; on account → Accounts Payable
Cash receipt: money in (cash sale, customer pays invoice, owner investment)
Cash payment: money out (expense, vendor, owner withdrawal)
Name the type first: entry and equation effect become easy
Special journals: each type maps to one

cards.say_it: The first transaction is a credit sale, so revenue is earned now even though the cash comes later, which is why we record Accounts Receivable instead of Cash.

core: Show increase or decrease on each side
detail: Steps: identify accounts, classify, up or down, write in the table
Table columns: Assets, Liabilities, Equity
Check: both sides change by the same net amount
Finish: total the columns
Revenue and expenses: go in the equity column
Judges want: a running table (mathematical depiction) of the impact
cards.formula: Change in Assets = Change in Liabilities + Change in Equity
cards.example: Best Coffee: A/R +100,000 | Equity +100,000; Inventory +36,000 | A/P +36,000; Cash +50,000 | Equity +50,000; Cash minus 23,500 | Equity minus 23,500. Totals: assets 162,500 = liabilities 36,000 + equity 126,500.
cards.say_it: Let me show you each transaction on the equation in a table so you can see that after every single one, the left side still equals the right side.
mistakes: Putting revenue in the assets column instead of showing its effect on equity

detail: Shows: date, amount, parties and purpose
Step one of the accounting cycle; evidence auditors check

Others: receipt (cash received), memorandum (internal, e.g. a correction), bank statement

cards.say_it: Before I record anything I want the source document, because it proves the amount and the date and it is what an auditor or the IRS will ask to see.
mistakes: Recording an entry from memory or a phone call with no supporting document

core: Used up each month: Insurance Expense
detail: Why an asset: payment covers several months of future benefit (current asset)

core: Imbalance = an error somewhere in the books
detail: Double entry: equal debits and credits keep assets = liabilities + equity
Imbalance causes: one sided entry, math error, posting mistake
Limit: balanced ≠ error free (error can hit both sides)
Use: first quick test
Errors left in: distort net income, equity, borrowing and expansion decisions
cards.example: Dance Frenzy: after correcting the intern's errors, assets $180,187 = liabilities $1,511 + owner's equity $178,676.
cards.say_it: The equation staying in balance is our proof that every transaction was recorded with both sides, which gives you confidence in the balance sheet you show the bank.
mistakes: Believing a balanced equation means there are no errors at all

Effect: Cash down, another asset up by the same amount
No effect: liabilities, equity, revenue, expense

cards.say_it: Buying supplies for cash is just an exchange of one asset for another, so it does not lower profit until the supplies are used.

core: Internal: inside the business (supplies used, depreciation)
detail: External parties: customers, vendors, lenders, employees, owner
External proof: usually an outside source document
Internal: no outside party; usually adjusting entries backed by a memorandum
Internal examples: supplies used, insurance expired, depreciation, accrued wages
Both: change accounts and must be recorded for accurate statements

cards.say_it: Depreciation is an internal transaction, so no one sends us a bill for it, and that is exactly why we must remember to record it as an adjusting entry.

detail: Why: right document → right classification
Sales on account: sales invoice; cash sales: sales receipt or register tape
Purchases: purchase requisition, purchase order, receiving report, vendor invoice
Payments: check or electronic payment record
Cash received: receipt or remittance slip

detail: Eight steps: analyze source documents, journalize, post, unadjusted trial balance, worksheet, adjust, statements, close
Last check: post-closing trial balance after closing entries
Repeats: every month, quarter or year for timely information
Path: every transaction ends up in the financial statements this way
cards.formula: Analyze, Journalize, Post, Trial balance, Worksheet, Adjust, Statements, Close (then post-closing trial balance)
cards.example: Best Coffee sells $100,000 of beans on account: the invoice is the source document, the sale is journalized (debit Accounts Receivable, credit Sales), posted to both ledger accounts, shows up on the trial balance, flows to the income statement, and Sales is closed to capital at year end.
cards.say_it: Every transaction you make travels the same path: source document, journal, ledger, trial balance, adjustments, statements and finally closing, so the cycle is how your raw receipts become reports you can trust.
mistakes: Order mix-up: adjusting entries come before the statements, closing entries after

core: Revenue and expenses in the right period
detail: Why: changes without a source document (time passes, assets used, amounts build up)
Prepaid (deferred) expenses: used up
Unearned (deferred) revenue: earned
Accrued expenses: owed, not yet paid or recorded; accrued revenue: earned, not yet billed
Estimates: depreciation, bad debts, warranties, inventory write-downs
Each entry: one income statement + one balance sheet account, never Cash
Where: general journal, posted before statements
cards.example: Monaco Company: one year of straight-line depreciation on $1,200 of office equipment over 3 years, debit Depreciation Expense $400, credit Accumulated Depreciation $400.
cards.say_it: An adjusting entry never touches cash; it just moves amounts between the balance sheet and the income statement so this period shows the right profit.
mistakes: Including Cash in an adjusting entry, or forgetting adjustments before preparing statements

detail: Purpose: temporary accounts reset to zero, balances moved to Owner's Capital
When: year end, so the next period starts fresh
Revenues: debit each revenue, credit Income Summary
Expenses: debit Income Summary, credit each expense
Income Summary: net income closed to Owner's Capital
Drawings: debit Owner's Capital, credit Drawings
Alternative: some close revenue and expenses directly to Capital
Never closed: permanent accounts (assets, liabilities, capital)
cards.formula: Revenue, Expenses, Income Summary, Drawings (REID)
cards.example: Dance Frenzy closes revenue straight to capital: debit Revenue $1,112,432, credit Owner's Capital $1,112,432.
cards.say_it: Closing entries reset the scoreboard: revenue and expenses start next year at zero, and this year's profit becomes part of your capital.
mistakes: Closing Cash or another permanent account

detail: Purpose: fixes a mistake already posted
Never erase or delete: destroys the audit trail
Debit: what was under-debited or over-credited
Credit: what was over-debited or under-credited
Explain: effect on assets, liabilities, equity, net income
Timing: any time an error is found (adjusting entries: period end, unrecorded items)
cards.formula: Correction = Correct entry minus Wrong entry (account by account)
cards.example: Monaco: $500 of supplies on account was recorded as Equipment $50 and Accounts Payable $50. Correction: debit Supplies $500, credit Equipment $50, credit Accounts Payable $450.
cards.say_it: Instead of erasing the mistake, I wrote one correcting entry for the difference so the records still show what happened and how it was fixed.
mistakes: Reversing and rewriting the whole entry when one difference entry would do, or deleting the original

Supplies: count what's left

detail: Start: find the difference in the trial balance or reconciliation
Divisible by 9: transposition (830 written as 380) or slide (450 written as 45)
Difference = twice an item: item probably on the wrong side
Difference = an item: entry likely missing on one side
Quick tests that impress judges
cards.formula: Difference / 9 = whole number suggests transposition or slide
cards.example: Monaco recorded an $830 payment as $380; difference $450, and 450 / 9 = 50, a sign of a transposition. Correction: debit Accounts Payable $450, credit Cash $450.
cards.say_it: The difference of $450 divides evenly by 9, which told me right away to look for two digits that were swapped.

cards.formula: Dr Expense, Cr Wages (or Interest, Utilities) Payable
cards.example: Employees earn $600 of wages on December 29 to 31 that will be paid January 4: debit Wages Expense $600, credit Wages Payable $600.
cards.say_it: Your employees already earned those wages this year, so the cost belongs to this year even though the paycheck goes out in January.

core: Adjusting: updates correct records at period end
detail: Adjusting: required even with no mistake
Adjusting examples: depreciation, expired insurance, accrued wages
Correcting: exists only because something was recorded wrongly
Cash: correcting entries can involve it; adjusting entries never do
Frequent judge question
cards.example: Monaco: moving the $1,200 of equipment out of Office Supplies is a correcting entry; recording $400 of depreciation on it is an adjusting entry.
cards.say_it: The correcting entry fixes the bookkeeper's mistake, while the depreciation entry would be needed even if every entry had been perfect.

cards.term: Effects of errors on the statements
core: Assets, liabilities, equity or net income
detail: Judge question: which errors would have changed income if undetected
Two balance sheet accounts (Supplies vs. Equipment): no net income change now
But: may change later depreciation
Expense or revenue account involved: net income and equity change
Withdrawal as expense: net income understated, total equity correct
Capitalizing vs. expensing: affects balance sheet and income
cards.example: Monaco: recording $1,200 of equipment as supplies, if expensed, understated assets and net income now, and $400 of yearly depreciation would never have been recorded.
cards.say_it: Only the errors that touched an expense account changed net income; the others just put the right amount in the wrong balance sheet account.

cards.term: Errors a trial balance cannot find
detail: Why missed: debits still equal credits
Wrong account: right column, so totals still match
Wrong amount: entered on both sides of a balanced entry
Never recorded or recorded twice: both sides affected equally
Compensating errors: offset each other
Still needed: source documents, account reviews, bank reconciliations, receivable and payable schedules
cards.example: A $200 haircut supply purchase debited to Equipment instead of Supplies still leaves Sam's trial balance equal at $53,450, but both accounts are wrong.
cards.say_it: A balanced trial balance tells us the math is right, but not that every number is in the right account, so we still review the source documents.

core: Temporary account used only during closing
detail: Revenues: credited into it; expenses: debited into it
Credit balance: net income; debit balance: net loss
Balance: then closed to Owner's Capital
Benefit: clear audit trail of net income
Optional: closing directly to Capital gives the same result
cards.example: If revenue is $27,100 and expenses are $19,990, Income Summary ends with a $7,110 credit, closed with debit Income Summary $7,110, credit Owner's Capital $7,110.
cards.say_it: The balance left in Income Summary after closing revenue and expenses is exactly this year's net income, which we then move to your capital.
mistakes: Leaving Income Summary with a balance after closing

detail: Permanent (real): balance sheet accounts continuing into next period
Temporary (nominal): one period of activity, reset to zero by closing
Income Summary: also temporary
Key to: spotting closing errors, building a post-closing trial balance
cards.example: Dance Frenzy's intern credited Cash for $145,000 as if closing it; Cash is permanent, so the correction is debit Cash $145,000, credit Owner's Capital $145,000.
cards.say_it: Cash is a permanent account, so its balance must carry into next year; only revenue, expenses and drawings get closed.

pis.text: Journalize and post closing entries

examples.title: Dance Frenzy dance studio: correcting an intern's closing entries and the post-closing trial balance

core: Proves ledger balanced for new period
detail: Last step of the accounting cycle
Contains: assets, contra assets, liabilities, Owner's Capital
Excludes: revenue, expense, drawings, Income Summary
Temporary account showing: closing was incomplete
Owner's Capital = beginning capital + net income minus drawings
cards.formula: Ending capital = Beginning capital + Net income minus Drawings
cards.example: Dance Frenzy corrected post-closing trial balance: Cash 145,000, Prepaid Insurance 4,332, Supplies 2,213, Furniture 4,321, Equipment 24,321 = 180,187 debits; Accounts Payable 1,511 + Owner's Capital 178,676 = 180,187 credits.
cards.say_it: A revenue account still showing on the post-closing trial balance was the sign that the intern never closed it.
mistakes: Including revenue or expense accounts on the post-closing trial balance

pis.text: Prepare a post-closing trial balance

examples.title: Dance Frenzy dance studio: correcting an intern's closing entries and the post-closing trial balance

core: Each balance in its normal column
detail: Heading: business name, Trial Balance, date
Order: assets, liabilities, capital, drawings, revenue, expenses
Column: debit or credit by normal balance
Equal totals: double rule them
Unequal: find the difference, search for errors
Contra accounts: column opposite their partner
cards.example: Sam's Barbershop: Cash 19,175, Supplies 1,625, Prepaid Insurance 2,100, Prepaid Rent 2,300, Accounts Receivable 1,050, Equipment 3,100, Drawings 4,110, Rent Expense 8,470, Supplies Expense 680, Advertising 970, Insurance 5,570, Utilities 4,300 = 53,450 debits; credits 4,900 + 21,450 + 27,100 = 53,450.
cards.say_it: I placed each account in its normal balance column, assets, drawings and expenses on the debit side and liabilities, capital and revenue on the credit side, and both columns total $53,450.
mistakes: Putting Drawings in the credit column because it is part of equity

pis.text: Prepare a trial balance

examples.title: Sam's Barbershop: preparing the year-end trial balance, its purpose, and errors it cannot detect

detail: Ten columns: debit and credit for each of five sections
Sections: trial balance, adjustments, adjusted trial balance, income statement, balance sheet
Income statement columns: revenue, expenses
Balance sheet columns: assets, liabilities, capital, drawings
Net income (or loss): difference of income statement columns
Net income: added to balance sheet credit column so it balances
Never given to outsiders
cards.formula: Net income = Income statement credit total minus Income statement debit total
cards.example: Coastal Surf Shop: Cash, Accounts Receivable, Merchandise Inventory and Accounts Payable go to the balance sheet columns; Sales and Cost of Goods Sold go to the income statement columns.
cards.say_it: The worksheet is my scratch pad that lets me see the effect of every adjustment and the net income before I prepare the formal statements.
mistakes: Extending Drawings to the income statement columns; it goes to the balance sheet debit column

Adjusted: includes adjusting entries; source for financial statements
Post-closing: after closing entries, permanent accounts only
Post-closing contents: assets, contra assets, liabilities, owner's capital
Post-closing proves: ledger ready for the new period
cards.example: Sam's $53,450 trial balance is unadjusted because prepaid rent and insurance have not yet been adjusted for the months used.
cards.say_it: This is the unadjusted trial balance, so before we prepare statements we still need to record the rent and insurance you used up this year.

detail: Prepared 3 times: unadjusted (after posting), adjusted, post-closing
Starting point: worksheet and financial statements
Won't balance if: unequal entry, miscalculated balance, wrong column
Balanced: necessary, but ≠ correct books
cards.formula: Total debit balances = Total credit balances
cards.example: Sam's Barbershop: debit balances (assets, drawings, expenses) total $53,450 and credit balances (Accounts Payable $4,900, Owner's Capital $21,450, Service Revenue $27,100) total $53,450.
cards.say_it: The trial balance proves our debits equal our credits, and it is the base we use to adjust the accounts and build your financial statements.

core: Earned, not yet billed or collected
detail: Examples: services finished but not invoiced, interest earned on a note receivable
Revenue recognition: work done, so revenue belongs to this period
Customer pays: debit Cash, credit the receivable
cards.formula: Dr Accounts (or Interest) Receivable, Cr Revenue
cards.example: A landscaper finishes a $1,500 job on December 30 but sends the invoice on January 3: debit Accounts Receivable $1,500, credit Service Revenue $1,500 on December 31.
cards.say_it: The job was finished in December, so the revenue is December revenue, even though the invoice goes out in January.

detail: Start: copy the unadjusted trial balance
Adjustments: matching letter for each entry's debit and credit
Adjusted balance: add or subtract
Extend: revenue and expenses to income statement; all others to balance sheet
Income statement credits > debits: difference = net income
Net income: add to balance sheet credit and income statement debit columns
Confirm: both pairs balance
cards.example: If income statement credits are $4,200 (Sales) and debits are $2,500 (Cost of Goods Sold), net income is $1,700, written in the income statement debit column and the balance sheet credit column.
cards.say_it: If the balance sheet columns balance after I add net income, I know the adjustments and extensions were done correctly.
mistakes: Adding net income to the balance sheet debit column instead of the credit column

core: Desktop: installed locally, bought or licensed
detail: Cloud pros: any location and device, several users, automatic updates and backups
More cloud pros: bank feeds, app integrations, lower upfront cost
Cloud cons: needs reliable internet, never-ending fees, data with a provider, conversion time
Desktop pros: works offline, one-time or periodic license, data on your computer
Desktop cons: one location, manual backups and updates, harder to share
Compare: total yearly cost, security, ease of training, growth needs
cards.example: Riverside Hardware: desktop $1,200 + $3,600 + ($6,000 / 3) = $6,800 a year vs. cloud $450 x 12 = $5,400, saving $1,400 a year plus remote access for both stores.
cards.say_it: The cloud system saves $1,400 a year and lets both stores work in the same books, and the staff training is simpler because the screens are the same everywhere.

detail: Automatic: records transactions, posts to general ledger
On demand: trial balances, statements, aging reports
Modules: sales, purchases, payables, inventory, payroll, bank reconciliation
Statements: sorted using chart of accounts numbering
Data in without retyping: bank feeds, point of sale integration, receipt capture
Benefits: speed, fewer math errors, real-time info, audit trails
Still needed: data review and access control
cards.example: EcoQuest numbers its accounts by group (100s assets, 200s liabilities, 300s equity, 400s revenue, 500s expenses) so the software sorts them into the right statements.
cards.say_it: Software does the posting and math, which frees us to analyze the results and make decisions instead of adding columns.

detail: Threats: hardware failure, theft, ransomware, fire
3 copies: the original plus two backups
2 media: for example a cloud service and an external drive
1 off site: at least one copy in another location
Cloud accounting: backs up automatically, but still export data regularly
Why export: provider could fail or the account could be locked
cards.example: Riverside Hardware follows the 3-2-1 rule and exports its full ledger every month, which answers the judge's question about what happens if the cloud company goes out of business.
cards.say_it: Even with a cloud system, we export a full copy of our books every month, so our records survive even if the provider does not.

core: Only the access their job needs
detail: Role-based access: cashier records sales, can't change prices or delete entries
Bookkeeper: enters bills, can't approve payments
Individual logins: audit trail of who did what
MFA: blocks most account takeovers
Employees leave: remove access immediately
Internal control: supports segregation of duties, guards against identity theft and fraud
cards.example: Riverside Hardware sets user access levels so each person sees and changes only what their job requires, and adds multifactor authentication before connecting the bank.
cards.say_it: Separate logins and access levels mean no single person can both create and approve a payment, which protects the business and the employees.

Analytics: trend and regression forecasts, scenario analysis, fraud detection
Full data sets: not just samples
Automation and AI: match transactions, flag unusual entries, read invoices
RegTech: anti-money-laundering monitoring, sanctions screening, audit trails
Jobs shift: toward analysis and advising; strong data controls needed

cards.say_it: A dashboard gives the board one view of all our key numbers and risks, so they can act in days instead of waiting for a quarterly report.

Benefit: less data entry, fewer errors

cards.say_it: Automating data entry gives us daily numbers instead of monthly ones, but someone still reviews the imports every week.

cards.term: Cutoff testing and search for unrecorded liabilities
core: Cutoff: year-end transactions in the right period
Unrecorded liabilities search: finds missing expenses
detail: Cutoff: shipping and receiving documents near year end vs recorded dates
Example: shipped in January, recorded in December → revenue overstated
Search: payments and invoices received after year end
Goal: old-year costs that were not recorded
Errors found: proposed adjusting entries
cards.example: Keystone: an unrecorded December utility invoice found in January payments leads to a proposed adjustment: Dr Utilities Expense, Cr Accounts Payable for the December amount. Its cutoff errors suggest expanding cutoff testing.
cards.say_it: We look at January payments because a December bill paid in January is still a December expense, and it's easy to miss.

pis.text: Describe auditing techniques/procedures
Conduct audit engagements

examples.title: Office Supplies Company: journalizing a credit sale and an accrued expense, revenue recognition and ethics of net-income bonuses
Keystone Components: first-year audit, materiality and a scope limitation

core: Internal: employees, test controls, improve operations
External: independent CPAs, opinion for outsiders
detail: Internal: reports to management and audit committee, year round
Internal: helps catch errors and fraud
External: independent CPA firm for banks, investors, regulators
External focus: fair presentation under GAAP, published opinion
External may use internal auditors' work, stays responsible for own opinion
cards.example: Tasty Dairy Delight: the internal auditor is an employee who tests internal controls; the external auditor is independent and gives the bank an opinion on the financial statements.
cards.say_it: Your internal auditor helps you run a tighter business; the external auditor is the independent outsider the bank trusts.
mistakes: Calling the external auditor an internal user because the auditor works with company records

pis.text: Distinguish between internal and external audits
Identify career opportunities in accounting

examples.title: JB Financial Accounting: middle school career day presentation on accounting careers, designations and professional organizations
Tasty Dairy Delight frozen yogurt shop: GAAP, internal vs. external users, and auditing
Keystone Components: first-year audit, materiality and a scope limitation

core: Sent directly to customers to verify balance owed
detail: Auditor controls sending and receiving: management can't alter replies
Positive: customer replies either way
Negative: reply only if the balance is wrong
No reply: alternative procedures (cash received after year end, invoices, shipping documents)
Management refuses: scope limitation, report to audit committee, can change opinion
cards.example: Keystone's CFO refuses confirmations for three customers owing $480,000, 16 times materiality, saying they always pay. The auditor tries alternative procedures and reports the restriction to the audit committee.
cards.say_it: Even if your customers always pay, we need evidence from outside the company, so either we confirm the balances or we check the cash received after year end.

pis.text: Describe auditing techniques/procedures
Conduct audit engagements

examples.title: Keystone Components: first-year audit, materiality and a scope limitation

core: Inherent risk × control risk × detection risk
detail: Audit risk: clean opinion on materially misstated statements
Inherent risk: misstatement likely before controls (complex estimates, cash)
Control risk: company's controls fail to catch it
Detection risk: auditor's tests miss it, only part the auditor controls
High inherent and control risk: lower detection risk with more, stronger substantive tests
cards.formula: Audit risk = Inherent risk x Control risk x Detection risk
cards.example: Illustration: acceptable audit risk 5%, inherent risk 100%, control risk 50%: detection risk = 0.05 / (1.00 x 0.50) = 10%. Keystone's cutoff errors raise risk, so the auditor expands cutoff testing.
cards.say_it: Because the cutoff errors show your controls aren't catching timing problems, we'll do more testing around year end.

pis.text: Describe auditing techniques/procedures
Conduct audit engagements

examples.title: Keystone Components: first-year audit, materiality and a scope limitation

core: Test a sample, not every transaction
Project results to the whole population
detail: Why: testing everything costs too much
Selection: statistical or by judgment
Large or unusual items: usually tested in full, sample the rest
Sample errors: projected to the population, compared with materiality
One reason for reasonable, not absolute, assurance
Data analytics: scan entire populations for unusual entries
cards.example: Illustration: an auditor tests all receivables over $50,000 and a random sample of 40 smaller ones; if the sample shows a 1% overstatement, it is projected across the remaining balance.
cards.say_it: We test a sample and the largest items, which gives strong evidence without checking every invoice, and that's why our assurance is reasonable rather than absolute.

pis.text: Describe auditing techniques/procedures

examples.title: Keystone Components: first-year audit, materiality and a scope limitation

detail: Inspection: examining documents or assets; observation: watching a process (inventory count)
Confirmation: written replies directly from third parties (customers, banks)
Inquiry: asking management and staff, never enough alone
Recalculation and reperformance: redoing computations or controls
Analytical procedures: ratios and trends to spot unusual changes
Vouching (records → documents): recorded items really happened
Tracing (documents → records): everything was recorded
Tests of controls: controls work; substantive tests: balances
cards.example: Keystone: confirm receivables, observe the inventory count, run analytical procedures on margins, vouch large sales to shipping documents, and trace January invoices back to December to find unrecorded liabilities.
cards.say_it: We can't just take management's word; inquiry has to be backed up with documents, confirmations and our own recalculations.

pis.text: Describe auditing techniques/procedures
Conduct audit engagements

examples.title: Keystone Components: first-year audit, materiality and a scope limitation

core: Independent in fact and in appearance
No financial or family ties that could bias
detail: In fact: judgment actually unbiased
In appearance: reasonable outsider would see it that way
Threats: owning client stock, loans, close family in key client roles
Threats: certain consulting services, long relationships
Response: remove the person, apply safeguards, document, or decline engagement
Without independence: opinion has no value to users
cards.example: A member of Keystone's audit team is the CFO's nephew. The firm removes him from the engagement right away and documents the action in the audit file.
cards.say_it: Even if he would be completely fair, the bank has to see us as independent, so he comes off the engagement today.

pis.text: Conduct audit engagements

examples.title: Keystone Components: first-year audit, materiality and a scope limitation

core: Materiality: misstatement size that could change a decision
Performance materiality: lower amount for planning tests
detail: Benchmark: e.g. 5 percent of pre-tax income (or % of revenue or assets)
Performance materiality: often 50 to 75 percent of overall materiality
Why lower: small undetected errors can add up to material
Misstatements found: totaled, compared with these levels
Immaterial ones: still correct or list on summary of uncorrected misstatements
Nature matters: a small fraud can be material
cards.formula: Materiality = Benchmark x Percentage (for example 5% x Pre-tax income); Performance materiality = Materiality x 75%
cards.example: Keystone: materiality 5% x 600,000 = $30,000; performance materiality 75% x 30,000 = $22,500. Misstatements found 12,000 + 3,000 = $15,000, below both, so not material, but management should still correct them.
cards.say_it: The $15,000 of errors is below our $30,000 materiality, so it won't change our opinion, but we still ask you to correct them.

pis.text: Conduct audit engagements
Describe auditing techniques/procedures

examples.title: Keystone Components: first-year audit, materiality and a scope limitation

detail: 1. Acceptance: independence, integrity, engagement letter (scope, timing, fees)
2. Planning: understand business and controls, set materiality, assess risks
3. Fieldwork: test controls, substantive procedures (confirmations, observation, cutoff, analytics)
4. Completion: evaluate misstatements, subsequent events, management representation letter
4. Completion: communicate with the audit committee
5. Reporting: issue the opinion
Workpaper documentation supports every step
cards.example: Keystone's first-year audit: confirm independence (the CFO's nephew is removed from the team), set $30,000 materiality, test cutoff and confirm receivables, propose the utility adjustment, then meet the audit committee before issuing the opinion.
cards.say_it: We're in fieldwork now; before we sign the opinion we'll summarize the misstatements and meet with your audit committee.

pis.text: Conduct audit engagements
Describe auditing techniques/procedures

examples.title: Keystone Components: first-year audit, materiality and a scope limitation

core: Unrecorded ones → summary of uncorrected misstatements
detail: Auditor writes correcting entry, asks management to record it
Why: statements are management's responsibility
Uncorrected items: totaled, compared with materiality alone and together
Material total uncorrected: no clean opinion
Management representation letter: confirms uncorrected items believed immaterial
cards.example: Keystone: the unrecorded December utility invoice becomes Dr Utilities Expense, Cr Accounts Payable; together with other errors the total is $15,000, below $30,000 materiality, but management is still asked to book them.
cards.say_it: These adjustments are small, but recording them now makes your statements cleaner and keeps them off our list of uncorrected misstatements.

pis.text: Conduct audit engagements

examples.title: Keystone Components: first-year audit, materiality and a scope limitation

detail: From circumstances: records destroyed in a fire
From management: refusing access to customers, records or staff
Management-imposed: serious, something may be hidden
First: try alternative procedures
Then: tell those charged with governance (usually the audit committee)
Still no evidence: modify the opinion or withdraw from the engagement
cards.example: Keystone's CFO blocks confirmations on $480,000 of receivables. The auditor documents it, tries subsequent cash receipts and shipping documents, and takes it to the audit committee.
cards.say_it: When management blocks evidence, it's a scope limitation, and we're required to take it to the audit committee before deciding on our opinion.

pis.text: Conduct audit engagements

examples.title: Keystone Components: first-year audit, materiality and a scope limitation

detail: Unmodified: fairly presented in all material respects
Qualified: fair except one material, not pervasive issue (misstatement or scope limitation)
Adverse: materially and pervasively misstated, not fairly presented
Disclaimer: not enough evidence for any opinion (material, pervasive scope limitation)
Lenders: usually require a clean opinion
cards.example: If Keystone's auditor still cannot verify the $480,000 of receivables, the result is a qualified opinion if the issue is material but not pervasive, or a disclaimer if it is pervasive, but not a clean opinion.
cards.say_it: If we can't verify those receivables, the best we can give is a qualified opinion, and your bank will notice that.

detail: Turns goals into numbers
Plan: how much to buy, produce, hire
Coordinate: sales, purchasing, production, finance on one forecast
Communicate targets; control spending (actual vs plan); evaluate managers
A forecast: revised as actual sales and costs come in
Small business start: monthly revenue and expense budget plus a cash budget
cards.example: Matrix Aluminum Piping builds a first-quarter purchases budget from the sales manager's forecast; the Society for Marketers compares budget with actual each quarter for its board.
cards.say_it: A budget is our plan in dollars: it tells purchasing what to order, tells finance how much cash we need, and lets us spot problems early by comparing actual results each month.

detail: Line up: budget and actual for each revenue and expense
Compute: difference in dollars and percent
Label: favorable (helps income) or unfavorable (hurts income)
Focus: large or controllable differences
Find cause: volume, price, waste, timing
Follow-up: assign to responsible manager, revise forecast if conditions changed
Volume far from plan: use a flexible budget, not the original static one
cards.example: If advertising was budgeted at $1,000 and actual was $1,400, that is a $400 (40%) unfavorable variance that needs an explanation, such as an unplanned campaign.
cards.say_it: Every month I compare actual results with the budget and explain any difference over 10%, so problems are caught while they are still small.

detail: Top-down: senior management sets targets, fast but may be unrealistic
Bottom-up: managers closest to work estimate, accurate, builds buy-in
Bottom-up downside: slower, may include padding
Incremental: last year adjusted by a percentage, simple but carries old waste
Zero-based: justify every cost from zero each period, finds waste but takes time
Rolling budgets: add a new month or quarter as each ends

cards.say_it: I recommend a bottom-up budget, because the sales manager knows our customers best and people commit to numbers they helped create.

cards.term: Budgeting backward from a profit target
detail: Use: find a spending limit for a cost such as payroll

cards.example: Harbor Fresh's truck should be worth $20,000 in 5 years. At 6%, PV = 20,000 x 0.7473 = $14,946.
cards.say_it: The truck's $20,000 resale value is worth only about $14,946 in today's dollars, and that is the number I subtract from the cost of buying.

core: PV = payment x PV annuity factor
detail: Ordinary annuity: pays at the end of each period
Examples: most loan and lease payments
Shortcut: multiply payment by the annuity factor instead of discounting each payment
Factor depends on: rate and number of periods
Result: what a stream of payments is worth today
Uses: lenders setting payments, lessee measuring a lease liability
cards.formula: PV of ordinary annuity = Payment x [1 minus (1 + r)^(minus n)] / r = Payment x PV annuity factor
cards.example: Harbor Fresh lease: 5 payments of $23,000 at 6%: 23,000 x 4.2124 = $96,885, even though total cash paid is $115,000.
cards.say_it: Five lease payments of $23,000 total $115,000 in cash, but their present value is $96,885, which is also the lease liability on the balance sheet.

core: Overhead assigned by actual activity use
detail: Traditional: one volume-based rate (labor or machine hours)
ABC steps: activity cost pools → cost driver per pool → activity rate → charge products
Best when: products differ in complexity or batch size
Mainly internal decision tool
GAAP inventory: still absorption costing (manufacturing costs only)
ABC with selling or admin costs: not directly in external statements
cards.example: Precision Machining: $60,000 / 100 setups = $600 per setup; $40,000 / 200 inspections = $200 each. Custom valves: (70 x $600) + (120 x $200) = $66,000 / 1,000 units = $66 overhead, $111 total cost.
cards.say_it: ABC charges the Custom Valve for the setups and inspections it really causes, which is why its true cost is $111, not $55.
mistakes: Saying ABC changes total overhead; it only changes how the same total is divided among products
cards.formula: Activity rate = Cost pool total / Total driver quantity

core: Factor that makes an activity's cost rise or fall
detail: Volume-based drivers: direct labor hours, machine hours, units
Volume drivers fit: overhead that rises with production volume
Other drivers: batches, complexity, customer demands
Examples: setups, inspections, purchase orders, engineering changes
Right driver: makes cost allocation accurate
cards.example: Precision Machining's setup costs are driven by the number of setups, not labor hours: custom valves are 10% of labor hours but 70% of setups.
cards.say_it: Setups cost money each time we change over a machine, so the number of setups, not labor hours, is the fair way to assign that cost.

detail: Prevention: stop defects before they happen (training, maintenance, better design)
Appraisal: find defects (inspection, testing)
Internal failure: defects caught before shipping (scrap, rework)
External failure: defects customers find (returns, replacements, warranty, lost sales, goodwill)
TQM logic: more prevention spending usually cuts failure costs by more
cards.formula: Cost of quality = Prevention + Appraisal + Internal failure + External failure
cards.example: EverGreen: $50,000 + $80,000 + $300,000 + $170,000 = $600,000, with 78% in failure costs. Adding $150,000 of prevention to cut failures 50% ($235,000) saves $85,000 a year.
cards.say_it: We spend 78% of our quality budget fixing mistakes, so moving money into prevention saves $85,000 a year before even counting customer goodwill.

core: Partly finished units → equivalent whole units
detail: Why: some units still in process at period end
Weighted average: equivalent units = units completed + (ending WIP units x percent complete)
Computed separately: materials vs conversion (labor + overhead)
Reason: materials often added at start, conversion happens evenly
Cost per equivalent unit: values completed units and ending WIP
cards.formula: Equivalent units (weighted average) = Units completed + (Ending WIP units x % complete)
cards.example: Illustration: 1,000 candles finished and 400 in process, 50% complete for conversion. Conversion equivalent units = 1,000 + 200 = 1,200. If wax is added at the start, materials equivalent units = 1,400. Conversion costs of $6,000 give $5 per equivalent unit.
cards.say_it: Four hundred half-finished candles count as two hundred whole candles of labor and overhead, so we spread the cost over 1,200 equivalent units.

core: Waste: extra inventory, waiting, defects, unneeded steps
detail: Organizes work around flow of value to the customer
Costs gathered by value stream (entire product flow), not job or department
Overhead allocations shrink: more costs directly traceable
Reports: emphasize non-financial measures
Less inventory: absorption income closer to variable costing income
cards.example: EverGreen Packaging's plant going lean would track cost per value stream for its box line and report cycle time and on-time delivery to managers alongside costs.
cards.say_it: Going lean means our reports should follow the whole product flow and show cycle time and defects, not just cost variances by department.

core: Costs averaged over many identical units
detail: Fits: continuous mass production (candles, paint, cereal, soft drinks, chemicals, aluminum pipe)
Costs collected by department (mixing, molding, packaging) per period
Cost per unit = department costs ÷ equivalent units produced
Partly finished units: converted into equivalent whole units
Vs job costing: no need to track each order separately
cards.formula: Cost per equivalent unit = Total department costs / Equivalent units
cards.example: Lumen Candle Company makes thousands of identical candles, so a process cost system that averages department costs over all candles made fits better than a job cost sheet for each candle.
cards.say_it: Since every candle is the same, we don't need a cost sheet per order; we average each department's costs over the candles it produced.

High-volume product: carries costs it doesn't cause

cards.say_it: Your Standard Valve has been paying $56,000 a year of the Custom Valve's costs, which is why you lose bids on one and lose money on the other.

core: Product costs: attach to inventory, expensed when sold
Period costs: expensed when they occur
detail: Product costs: direct materials, direct labor, manufacturing overhead
Product costs: asset in inventory, then cost of goods sold
Period costs: selling, advertising, administrative, expensed right away (both methods)
Only switching cost: fixed manufacturing overhead
Absorption: product cost; variable costing: period cost
This timing explains different income under the two methods
cards.example: Lumen: the $18,000 of selling and administrative cost is a period cost under both methods. The $40,000 of fixed factory overhead is a product cost under absorption ($8,000 of it waits in ending inventory) and a period cost under variable costing.
cards.say_it: Office and selling costs are expensed right away either way; the only difference is whether factory fixed overhead waits in inventory.

cards.term: Reconciling absorption and variable costing income
core: Difference = fixed overhead per unit × change in inventory units
detail: Production > sales: fixed overhead deferred in inventory, absorption income higher
Sales > production: deferred fixed overhead released, variable costing income higher
Production = sales: same income
Total spending identical: only timing of fixed overhead expense differs
cards.formula: Absorption income minus Variable income = Fixed MOH per unit x (Units produced minus Units sold)
cards.example: Lumen: 22,000 minus 14,000 = $8,000 = $4 x (10,000 minus 8,000). If only 8,000 candles were made, fixed overhead would be $5 each, COGS 8,000 x $11 = $88,000, and absorption income would be $14,000, the same as variable costing.
cards.say_it: The extra $8,000 of absorption profit isn't new money; it's $4 of fixed overhead sitting in each of the 2,000 unsold candles.

core: Contribution margin minus traceable fixed costs
Best measure of a segment's long-run profit
detail: Segment: division, product line, store or region with its own cost and profit report
Shows: what the segment adds toward common costs and profit
Evaluate managers on: segment margin (contribution margin for short-run decisions)
Not on: net income after arbitrary allocations they can't control
cards.formula: Segment margin = Sales minus Variable costs minus Traceable fixed costs
cards.example: FitTech Smart Shoes: $100,000 minus $60,000 = $40,000.
cards.say_it: I would evaluate the shoe division manager on the $40,000 segment margin, because the $65,000 of headquarters cost is outside her control.

core: Expected quantity and price per input per unit
detail: Standard cost card: materials quantity and price, labor hours and rate, overhead rate
Budget building block: budgeted cost = budgeted units x standard cost per unit
After period: actual vs standard cost allowed for actual output
Variances: investigated
Works with: job or process systems
Supports: pricing and cost control
cards.formula: Standard cost per unit = Sum of (Standard quantity x Standard price) for each input
cards.example: Crumb & Co. Bakery standard per loaf: flour 2 lbs x $0.50 = $1.00; labor 0.1 hour x $15 = $1.50; variable overhead $0.50; standard variable cost $3.00 per loaf.

mistakes: Changing standards to make unfavorable variances disappear

core: Traceable: exist only because of a segment
Common: support whole company, remain if segment dropped
detail: Traceable examples: division's own supervisors, its advertising, equipment only it uses
Common examples: headquarters rent, CEO's salary, company-wide software
Allocation: common costs often spread by sales or floor space
Allocation doesn't change the total the company pays
Trap: allocations can make a profitable segment look unprofitable
cards.example: FitTech: shoe supervisors and shoe advertising ($60,000) are traceable; headquarters rent and the CEO salary allocated to shoes ($65,000) are common.
cards.say_it: The headquarters costs do not disappear if we close Smart Shoes; they just move to the other two divisions.

core: Value stream: costs assigned to whole product flows
Backflush: costs recorded at end of production
detail: Value stream costing: all flow costs (labor, machines, materials, support) ÷ units shipped
Avoids: detailed job tracking and overhead allocations
Backflush (with JIT): skips recording each WIP step
Backflush: standard costs assigned when goods finished or sold
Why it works: inventory is so small
Both: less bookkeeping, match how a lean plant runs
cards.example: EverGreen's corrugated box line could be one value stream: total weekly costs of the line divided by boxes shipped gives the cost per box without tracking each order.
cards.say_it: With almost no inventory, we don't need to track every job through work in process; costing the whole value stream is simpler and just as useful.

core: Unit cost = only variable manufacturing costs
All fixed overhead expensed in the period
detail: Also called: direct costing
Unit cost = direct materials + direct labor + variable overhead
Fixed manufacturing overhead: period cost, expensed in full regardless of units sold
Contribution format: sales − all variable costs = CM, − all fixed costs = operating income
Internal use: CVP, pricing, performance evaluation
Income moves with sales, not production
Not allowed for GAAP external reports
cards.formula: Variable unit cost = DM + DL + Variable MOH
cards.example: Lumen Candle: unit cost $6. Sales $120,000 minus variable costs $56,000 = contribution margin $64,000; minus fixed costs $50,000 = operating income $14,000.
cards.say_it: Variable costing shows profit only when candles are sold, which makes it the better tool for judging the manager and making decisions.

core: Fixed costs ÷ contribution margin per unit
detail: At break-even: total revenue = total costs (variable + fixed)
Meaning: units to sell before any profit is earned
Round up to the next whole unit (no fractional units sold)
Starting point: compare with expected sales to judge risk
Next step: plan for a target profit
cards.formula: Break-even units = Fixed costs / (Price minus Variable cost per unit)

mistakes: Dividing fixed costs by the selling price instead of the contribution margin

core: How price, volume and cost changes affect profit
detail: Relationship: profit = (price x units) minus (variable cost per unit x units) minus fixed costs
What-ifs: cut price, add an employee, sell 10% more, lease a new machine
Uses: profit planning, pricing, production volume, break-even
Assumption: costs split into fixed and variable
Assumption: prices and unit costs constant within the relevant range
cards.formula: Profit = (Price minus Variable cost per unit) x Units minus Fixed costs
cards.example: Jotter at 30,000 units and $4.75: (4.75 minus 1.50) x 30,000 minus 19,000 = $78,500 profit; at 10,000 units only $13,500.
cards.say_it: CVP shows that producing 30,000 notebooks earns $78,500 versus $13,500 at 10,000, because the fixed costs are spread over more units.

core: Variable: total changes with volume, same per unit
Fixed: same in total, per unit falls as volume rises
Holds only within the relevant range
detail: Base of CVP, budgets and pricing
Variable: materials, per-unit direct labor, commissions, packaging, food ingredients
Fixed: rent, insurance, salaried supervisors, equipment rental, depreciation
Higher volume: fixed cost per unit falls, total cost per unit drops
Relevant range: normal operating range where cost structure stays the same
cards.example: Jotter Manufacturers: variable cost $1.50 per notebook at every volume; fixed costs $19,000 total, so fixed cost per unit is $1.90 at 10,000, $0.95 at 20,000 and $0.63 at 30,000. Rocking Ribs: rent, insurance and utilities of $4,300 are fixed; meat and payroll are variable.
cards.say_it: Your $19,000 of fixed costs don't change with volume, so every extra notebook spreads them thinner and lowers the cost of each unit.
mistakes: Saying fixed cost per unit is constant, or treating a per-unit fixed cost as if it changes total cost

core: How far sales can fall before break-even
detail: Measures risk
Shown in units, dollars, or % of expected sales
Large margin: sales can drop a lot before a loss
Small margin: even a mild slowdown is dangerous
Use: recommending a production quantity, presenting a forecast to a lender
cards.formula: Margin of safety = Expected sales minus Break-even sales; Margin of safety % = Margin of safety / Expected sales
cards.example: Jotter at 30,000 notebooks x $4.75 = $142,500 of sales; break-even about $27,769; margin of safety about $114,731, or about 80% of sales.
cards.say_it: Even if sales fell by 80%, we would still break even, so this plan has a very comfortable margin of safety.

core: How sharply profit changes when sales change
detail: Degree of operating leverage = contribution margin ÷ operating income
DOL of 2: sales up 10 percent → operating income up about 20 percent
Same DOL of 2: sales down 10 percent → income down about 20 percent
Mostly fixed costs (gyms, factories): big gains when sales rise, risky when they fall
Mostly variable costs: safer, profit grows more slowly
Connects CVP to business risk
cards.formula: Degree of operating leverage = Contribution margin / Operating income
cards.example: Jotter at 30,000 notebooks: CM 30,000 x 3.25 = $97,500; operating income 97,500 minus 19,000 = $78,500; leverage 97,500 / 78,500 = about 1.24, so a 10% sales increase raises income about 12.4%.
cards.say_it: Because most of our costs are fixed, a slow season hits profit harder than sales, which is why the low-season staffing plan matters so much.

cards.term: Relevant costs for a special order
core: Accept if price > costs that change because of the order
Only if regular sales are not lost
detail: Relevant costs: future costs that differ between choices
Idle capacity: variable production costs + extra costs for the order
Irrelevant: fixed overhead paid anyway, costs that won't occur (unpaid commissions)
Compare: price vs relevant cost per unit, × units
Full capacity: add lost contribution margin on displaced sales (opportunity cost)
Then: weigh qualitative risks
cards.formula: Change in operating income = (Special price minus Relevant cost per unit) x Units minus Opportunity cost
cards.example: Velocity Athletic Gear: relevant cost = materials $15 + labor $10 + variable overhead $5 + printing $2 = $32. At $35: $3 x 5,000 = $15,000 more operating income. The lowest acceptable price is $32. At full capacity the order would displace regular sales and lower income.
cards.say_it: The $38 product cost includes $8 of fixed overhead we pay anyway, so any price above our $32 relevant cost adds profit, $15,000 on this order.
mistakes: Rejecting the order because the price is below full (absorption) cost per unit

core: Opportunity: benefit given up, always relevant
detail: Sunk example: money already paid for equipment, no decision changes it, ignore it
Opportunity costs: not recorded in the accounts, but they matter
Full capacity: one use gives up the contribution margin of another
Idle capacity: no opportunity cost
Explains most special order, make or buy, transfer pricing answers
cards.example: Velocity has 10,000 jerseys of idle capacity, so the 5,000-jersey order has no opportunity cost. If the plant were full, the lost margin on regular jerseys would be an opportunity cost; Northwind's minimum transfer price at full capacity rises from $8 to $13 for the same reason.
cards.say_it: What we paid for the machines is sunk and doesn't matter; what matters is whether this order pushes out regular sales, and with idle capacity it doesn't.

detail: Small fee, short period: can be very expensive per year
Period rate: cost / cash actually received
Annualize: multiply by number of such periods in a year
Puts on one yearly basis: factoring fees, skipped discounts, short-term loans, bank annual rate
cards.formula: Annual rate = (Cost / Cash received) x (360 / Days)
cards.example: Swift Route factoring: $8,000 fee / $192,000 received = 4.2% for 60 days; x 360/60 = 6 periods, about 25% a year, versus 9% for the bank loan.
cards.say_it: Factoring costs about 25% a year compared with 9% for the loan, so we would only choose it to protect our debt covenant.

core: Otherwise full amount due in 30 days
detail: Credit terms: when payment is due, and any discount for paying early
Hidden cost: skipping the discount = paying 2% more to use the money 20 extra days
Annual cost: about 37% a year
Rule: almost always take the discount, even if borrowing at a normal bank rate
n/30 alone: full amount due in 30 days, no discount
cards.formula: Annual cost of skipping the discount = discount % / (100% minus discount %) x 365 / (full days minus discount days)
cards.example: Locally Picked sells $1,000 on June 10 with terms 2/10, n/30: the grocery store pays $980 by June 20 or $1,000 by July 10. Skipping the discount costs 2/98 x 365/20 = about 37% a year.
cards.say_it: Taking the 2% discount is like earning 37% a year on our money, so it is worth paying early even if we use our line of credit to do it.
mistakes: Thinking 2% is too small to matter: annualized it is far more expensive than a bank loan

detail: Truth in Lending Act: lenders must disclose APR and finance charge
Purpose: compare offers on the same basis
APR vs stated rate: APR usually higher, includes some required fees
Credit cards: often above 20%
Mortgages and auto loans: lower, collateral reduces lender risk
Compare: APRs and total finance charges, not monthly payments alone
cards.example: Two $10,000 loans both at 7% interest: one charges a $500 fee, so its APR is higher and it costs more in total.
cards.say_it: I compare financing offers by APR and total finance charge, because a lower monthly payment can hide a longer term and more interest.

detail: Debt-to-income: monthly debt payments / gross monthly income, lenders prefer under about 36%
First: list every debt with balance and rate
Then: pay minimums on all
Avalanche: extra money to highest rate first, saves the most interest
Snowball: smallest balance first, builds motivation
Also: avoid new borrowing, consolidate at a lower rate, contact lenders early
Businesses watch: debt ratio, debt-to-equity, loan covenants
cards.formula: Debt-to-income = Monthly debt payments / Gross monthly income
cards.example: Monthly debts $900 / gross income $3,000 = 30% debt-to-income, an acceptable level.
cards.say_it: Bayside already finances 80% of its assets with debt, so adding a large line of credit would make its debt harder to control, not easier.

core: Interest = Principal x Rate x Time
Cost of credit = total interest + fees
detail: Cost of credit: everything paid beyond the amount borrowed
Fees: origination, late, annual
Simple interest inputs: principal, annual rate, time in years
Short business loans: banks often use a 360-day year, time = days / 360
Comparing loans: total cost and annual rate, not just the monthly payment
cards.formula: Interest = Principal x Annual rate x Time (in years, or days / 360)
cards.example: Swift Route Logistics: $200,000 x 9% x 60/360 = $3,000 of interest on a 60-day bank loan, versus an $8,000 factoring fee.
cards.say_it: The bank loan costs $3,000 for 60 days, which is $5,000 less than factoring, so cost alone favors the loan; the question is whether the extra debt breaks our covenant.
mistakes: Using the full annual rate for a 60-day loan instead of multiplying by 60/360

Others: limits on dividends or owner withdrawals, on-time financial statements

core: Tie to measures hard to manipulate
Reward what's best for the company
detail: Revenue-based: encourages sales, ignores costs

core: Locks exchange rate for a future date
detail: Hedging: taking an offsetting position to reduce risk
Forward contract: with a bank, rate fixed today for a set future delivery date
Currency rises: hedge saves money
Currency falls: hedge costs more than not hedging
Either way: cost known on order day, protects margins and budgets
Risk control, not speculation; follow a written policy
cards.example: Forward rate $1.09: 50,000 x 1.09 = $54,500. It saves $500 compared with the $55,000 paid at $1.10, but if the euro had fallen to $1.05 the unhedged cost would have been $52,500, so the hedge would have cost $2,000 more.
cards.say_it: Sometimes the hedge will cost us money, but we pay that price for knowing our exact cost when we set our selling prices.
mistakes: Judging a hedge only by whether it "won" after the fact

core: Debt ratio = total liabilities / total assets

Shows: how much of the business is financed with borrowed money

Investing: buying or selling equipment, buildings, investments
Financing: borrowing and repaying loan principal, owner investments and withdrawals
Financing also: issuing stock, buying back stock, paying dividends
Healthy mature business: positive operating cash flow funds investing
Start-up: often negative operating cash flow funded by financing
cards.example: Harbor Fresh: truck purchase $100,000 is investing (cash out); the $100,000 loan is financing (cash in); each year's $20,000 principal repayment is financing (out); the interest is operating (out) under U.S. GAAP.
cards.say_it: Buying the truck is an investing outflow and the loan is a financing inflow, so the two offset and our operating cash flow stays the real test of the business.

detail: Sale on account: raises net income before cash arrives
Unpaid bill: lowers net income before cash leaves
Inventory purchase: uses cash before it becomes an expense
Depreciation: lowers income, no cash paid

detail: Pressure (motive): debts, lifestyle, bonus targets, personal problems
Opportunity: weak controls, e.g. one person handling everything
Rationalization: self-story (underpaid, will pay it back)
Management can rarely remove pressure or rationalization
Can remove opportunity: internal controls are the main defense
Fraud risk assessment: check all three sides
cards.example: Bella Vista: pressure (a new car and possible money problems), opportunity (Dana handles cash, records and reconciliation with no review and uses the signature stamp), rationalization (eight years of service, may feel underpaid). All three are present, so the risk is high.
cards.say_it: You can't control Dana's finances, but you can remove the opportunity, and that is what internal controls do.

detail: Collusion: two employees together defeat segregation of duties
Override: managers can bypass controls
Human error: mistakes, carelessness when controls feel routine
Cost: control shouldn't cost more than the risk it reduces
Response: monitor and update controls; audits test them, never assume
cards.example: Even after Bella Vista separates duties, a cashier and a manager could collude on fake voids, so the owner's weekly review of void reports remains important.
cards.say_it: No system is perfect, so we keep monitoring; a weekly look at the reports is what catches collusion or overrides.

cards.say_it: A control only works if someone keeps doing it, so I'd put each one on a checklist with a name and a date next to it.

cards.term: Comparing inventory methods when costs rise
core: FIFO: highest profit and ending inventory
detail: Cost flow assumptions: not physical flows
Rising costs, FIFO: lowest COGS, highest gross profit, taxes, ending inventory
Rising costs, LIFO: the reverse
Falling costs: results flip
Choice based on: matching, tax effect, industry practice, physical flow
Then: use it consistently
cards.example: Sneaker reseller with rising costs: gross profit FIFO $320 > weighted average $202.50 > LIFO $100. Dene Company: FIFO ending inventory $1,260 vs. LIFO $900, a $360 difference.
cards.say_it: Because your costs have been rising, FIFO reports the highest profit and LIFO the lowest, so the method you choose changes your taxes but not your cash from sales.
mistakes: Forgetting that the ranking reverses when costs are falling

core: Beginning inventory + net purchases − ending inventory
detail: Periodic system: count inventory at period end, compute COGS by formula

Goods available split: sold (COGS) vs left (ending inventory)
Largest merchandiser expense: net sales − COGS = gross profit
Ending inventory error: flows straight into COGS and net income
cards.formula: COGS = Beginning inventory + Net purchases minus Ending inventory = Cost of goods available for sale minus Ending inventory
cards.example: Dene Company: goods available $6,300 for 1,000 units; FIFO ending inventory $1,260, so COGS = 6,300 minus 1,260 = $5,040.
cards.say_it: Every dollar we put into ending inventory is a dollar that isn't in cost of goods sold, which is why an accurate count matters so much.
mistakes: Adding ending inventory instead of subtracting it

Periodic: updated only after a physical count

Perpetual: each sale records Cost of Goods Sold; balance always current

Periodic: purchases to a Purchases account, COGS calculated at period end

cards.example: Mason's seafood market records each sale and its cost as it happens (perpetual); Dene Company figures COGS at month end from a count (periodic).

core: Beginning WIP + manufacturing costs − ending WIP
detail: Three inventories: raw materials, work in process, finished goods
Total manufacturing costs = DM used + direct labor + manufacturing overhead
COGM (finished this period): moves to Finished Goods
COGS = beginning finished goods + COGM − ending finished goods
Or: COGS = units sold x unit product cost
Absorption costing: fixed overhead part of product costs
cards.formula: COGM = Beginning WIP + (DM + DL + MOH) minus Ending WIP; COGS = Beginning FG + COGM minus Ending FG
cards.example: Illustration: beginning WIP $10,000 + manufacturing costs $120,000 (DM 50,000 + DL 30,000 + MOH 40,000) minus ending WIP $15,000 = COGM $115,000. COGS = 20,000 + 115,000 minus 25,000 = $110,000. Lumen Candle: 8,000 sold x $10 absorption cost = $80,000.
cards.say_it: For a manufacturer, cost of goods sold comes from what we finished this period, adjusted for the finished candles still in the warehouse.

core: FOB shipping point: buyer owns and pays freight from shipment
FOB destination: seller does until delivery
detail: Freight in (buyer pays, incoming goods): part of inventory cost
Perpetual freight in: debit Merchandise Inventory
Freight out (seller delivers): selling expense (Delivery Expense)
Goods in transit: FOB terms decide whose inventory at year end
Matters for: accurate count and cutoff
cards.example: A surf shop buys boards FOB shipping point and pays $150 shipping: debit Merchandise Inventory $150, credit Cash $150, so the boards cost $150 more.
cards.say_it: Because the terms are FOB shipping point, the boards became ours when they left the vendor, so the freight is part of their cost.

cards.term: Lower of cost or net realizable value
detail: U.S. GAAP (ASC 330): FIFO and average cost at lower of cost or NRV
LIFO: lower of cost or market
NRV = expected selling price minus costs to complete, sell and ship
Write-down: adjusting entry, raises COGS (or separate loss)
Effect: cuts gross profit and net income
U.S. GAAP: written-down amount = new cost, no reversal
IFRS: reversal allowed up to original cost
cards.formula: NRV = Selling price minus costs to sell | Write-down = (Cost minus NRV) x units
cards.example: Apex Electronics: NRV $350 minus $20 = $330 vs. cost $400; write-down $70 x 1,000 = $70,000: debit Cost of Goods Sold $70,000, credit Merchandise Inventory $70,000; inventory now $330,000.
cards.say_it: Inventory cannot sit on the balance sheet above the cash it will bring in, so we write it down to $330 a unit, and under U.S. GAAP we cannot write it back up later.
mistakes: Reversing a write-down when prices recover under U.S. GAAP

detail: Step 1: event happened? (an order alone is not a sale)
Step 2: name the accounts affected
Step 3: classify (asset, liability, equity, revenue, expense, contra)
Step 4: increase or decrease
Step 5: debits increase assets, expenses, drawings; credits increase liabilities, equity, revenue

DEALER: Liabilities, Equity, Revenue up with credits

core: Best estimate in range → accrue it
No amount more likely → accrue minimum, disclose the rest
detail: U.S. GAAP: low end accrued, disclose loss could reach top of the range
IFRS (IAS 37): uses the midpoint instead
Recording the maximum to be safe: not allowed
Why not maximum: overstates the liability, understates income without support

detail: Market rate > stated rate: sells at a discount (below face)
Market rate < stated rate: sells at a premium (above face)
Discount or premium: amortized over the life, adjusts interest expense
Issued below face: debit Cash + Discount on Bonds Payable, credit Bonds Payable (face)
Reported: net of the discount (carrying value)
cards.formula: Cash interest = Face value x Stated rate x Time | Interest expense = Cash interest + Discount amortized
cards.example: $100,000 of 10-year 6% bonds sold at 98: debit Cash $98,000, debit Discount on Bonds Payable $2,000, credit Bonds Payable $100,000. Semiannual cash interest $3,000; straight-line discount amortization $2,000 / 20 = $100; interest expense $3,100.
cards.say_it: Investors paid only $98,000 because our 6% rate is below the market rate, so the $2,000 discount becomes extra interest expense over the bond's life.

cards.term: Loss contingencies: probable, reasonably possible, remote
detail: Loss contingency: possible loss from a past event, depending on a future event (e.g. lawsuit outcome)
U.S. GAAP (ASC 450) questions: how likely? can it be reasonably estimated?
Probable and estimable: Dr Loss, Cr Estimated Liability, plus describe in the notes
Reasonably possible (or probable but not estimable): no entry, disclose nature and possible amount
Remote: no entry, usually no disclosure
Gain contingencies: not recorded until realized
cards.example: Nexus Appliances: the probable class action is accrued; the reasonably possible $100,000 patent claim is disclosed only; the remote distributor claim is ignored.
cards.say_it: Recording the class action is not admitting guilt; it tells lenders and investors about a probable cash outflow so they are not misled.

core: Beginning balance + accruals − amounts settled = ending balance
detail: Why: numbers alone don't explain warranty terms, refund policies, pending lawsuits

cards.say_it: Our note will show the warranty liability rolling from zero to $3,500, so investors can see exactly how much we expect to spend on future repairs.

Equal payment series: annuity factor

detail: Right of return: revenue includes only what the company expects to keep
Period end: estimate returns on recent sales
Sales Returns and Allowances: contra revenue account
Refund Liability: recorded at selling price
Estimated Inventory Returns: asset at cost, since returned goods can be resold
Net effect on income: lost gross profit on the expected returns
cards.formula: Refund liability = Expected returns x Selling price; Returns asset = Expected returns x Cost
cards.example: Voltra: 60 December bikes x 5% = 3 bikes. Dr Sales Returns and Allowances 4,500, Cr Refund Liability 4,500 (3 x $1,500). Dr Estimated Inventory Returns 2,700, Cr Cost of Goods Sold 2,700 (3 x $900). Net income falls by $1,800.

mistakes: Forgetting the returns asset (overstates the effect on income) or ignoring expected returns entirely

core: Recorded when the obligation is actually incurred
detail: Restructuring: closing a plant, exiting a product line, cutting staff

core: Expense estimated on this year's sales
Liability = accrued expense − repairs already performed
detail: Method 1: sales dollars × estimated warranty rate
Method 2: units sold × expected repair rate × average cost per repair
Estimated Warranty Liability: beginning balance + expense accrued − repairs performed
Repairs: not a second expense, they use up the liability already recorded
Ending balance: (usually current) liability on the balance sheet
cards.formula: Warranty expense = Sales x Warranty rate (or Units x Repair rate x Cost per repair); Ending liability = Beginning + Expense accrued minus Repairs performed
cards.example: Nexus Appliances: 500,000 x 4% = $20,000 expense; repairs $12,000; ending liability 0 + 20,000 minus 12,000 = $8,000. Voltra: 400 x 6% = 24 bikes x $250 = $6,000; repairs $2,500; ending liability $3,500.
cards.say_it: We accrue $20,000 of warranty expense for this year's sales, and the $12,000 of repairs simply reduces that liability, leaving $8,000 for repairs still to come.
mistakes: Recording repairs as warranty expense after already accruing it: counts the cost twice

core: DDB: 2 × straight-line rate on remaining book value
detail: Straight-line = (cost − salvage value) / useful life
DDB rate = 2 / useful life, applied to beginning book value
DDB: salvage ignored in formula, stop when book value reaches salvage
Entry: Dr Depreciation Expense, Cr Accumulated Depreciation
Book value = cost − accumulated depreciation
Same total over life: DDB moves expense earlier
Choose by how the asset is used up, not to manage earnings; tax uses MACRS
cards.formula: Straight-line = (Cost minus Salvage) / Life; DDB = (2 / Life) x Beginning book value
cards.example: Titan Hauling tractor, $120,000 cost, $20,000 salvage, 5 years: straight-line $20,000 a year. DDB 40%: Year 1 $48,000, Year 2 40% x 72,000 = $28,800, book value $43,200.
cards.say_it: Double-declining-balance doesn't lower total depreciation; it just records more of it in the early years when the tractor works hardest.
mistakes: Subtracting salvage value before applying the DDB rate, or depreciating below salvage value

cards.formula: Annual depreciation = (Cost minus Salvage value) / Useful life
cards.example: Monaco: $1,200 / 3 = $400 a year. Titan: ($120,000 minus $20,000) / 5 = $20,000. Timber Valley with a 10 year life: $50,000 / 10 = $5,000, so yearly net income would be $45,000 instead of $40,000.
cards.say_it: With a 10 year life the yearly depreciation drops to $5,000, so each year shows more profit, but the total cost is the same.
mistakes: Forgetting to subtract salvage value

Tangible: depreciated (except land)
Limited-life intangibles: amortized

cards.say_it: The drones are tangible long-term assets, so we spread their cost over their useful life with depreciation instead of expensing them all at once.

core: Spreads limited-life intangible cost over its life
detail: Intangibles: no physical form
Examples: patents (legal life 20 years), copyrights, trademarks, franchises, software, customer lists
Purchased: recorded at cost
Internally developed (research costs): mostly expensed under U.S. GAAP
Indefinite life (goodwill, some trademarks): not amortized, impairment tested
Private companies: may elect to amortize goodwill
cards.formula: Annual amortization = Cost / Useful life
cards.example: A company buys a patent for $60,000 with a 10 year useful life: debit Amortization Expense $6,000, credit Patent (or Accumulated Amortization) $6,000 each year.
cards.say_it: The patent will protect our product for 10 years, so we expense $6,000 of its cost each year it helps us earn revenue.
mistakes: Amortizing goodwill as a public company, or using legal life when useful life is shorter

core: Book method doesn't change cash taxes
detail: MACRS: Modified Accelerated Cost Recovery System (IRS)
MACRS rules: set recovery periods, no salvage value
Faster deductions: bonus depreciation, Section 179
Book method: should reflect how the asset is used up
Book vs tax difference: temporary, creates deferred tax on the balance sheet
Picking a book method to manage earnings: unethical

core: Natural resource cost spread over units extracted
detail: Resources: timber, oil, gas, minerals, used up as removed
Rate per unit = (cost minus salvage) ÷ total estimated units
Depletion = rate × units extracted
Extracted, not yet sold: cost stays in inventory
cards.formula: Depletion rate = (Cost minus Salvage) / Total estimated units | Depletion = Rate x Units extracted

cards.say_it: We charge depletion for each ton we dig out, because the pit is literally being used up as we sell the gravel.

detail: Gain or loss = cash received minus book value
Entry: debit Cash and Accumulated Depreciation, credit asset at original cost
Difference: credit Gain on Sale or debit Loss on Sale
Multi-step income statement: other revenues and gains (or other expenses and losses)
Placement: below operating income
Scrapped, no proceeds: loss = book value
cards.formula: Gain (loss) = Proceeds minus Book value

cards.say_it: We sold the tractor for $1,800 more than its book value, so we record a gain, and it appears below operating income because selling tractors is not our main business.
mistakes: Comparing the sale price with original cost instead of book value

core: Beginning book value × twice straight-line rate
detail: Accelerated: assets that lose usefulness quickly
Rate = 2 / useful life
Salvage: ignored in the formula
Floor: book value never below salvage; last years limited
Income: lower early, higher later
Total over life: same as straight-line
cards.formula: DDB depreciation = Beginning book value x (2 / Useful life)
cards.say_it: Double-declining puts more cost in the early years, when the tractor is newest and most productive, but it can never take book value below the $20,000 salvage value.

core: Carrying value not recoverable from future cash flows
detail: U.S. GAAP: ASC 360
Triggering events: new regulations, damage, falling demand
Step 1 (recoverability): carrying value vs undiscounted future cash flows
Cash flows lower: asset is impaired
Step 2 (measurement): loss = carrying value minus fair value
Loss: non-cash charge in operating income
After: written-down value = new depreciation basis
Reversal: not allowed under U.S. GAAP, allowed under IFRS
cards.formula: Impaired if Carrying value > Undiscounted cash flows | Loss = Carrying value minus Fair value
cards.example: Horizon drones: carrying value $150,000 > cash flows $140,000, so impaired; loss $150,000 minus $110,000 = $40,000: debit Impairment Loss $40,000, credit Accumulated Depreciation $40,000. Next year depreciation $110,000 / 4 = $27,500 instead of $37,500.
cards.say_it: If the cash flows had been $160,000, the drones would pass Step 1 and we would record no impairment at all, even though fair value is lower.
mistakes: Using fair value in Step 1 instead of undiscounted cash flows
