core: Overhead: ongoing costs of running the business
Operating: materials, labor, machinery to deliver the product
detail: Overhead: fairly static, tied to general business functions
Overhead examples: rent, utilities, insurance, accounting and admin salaries, facility costs
Operating: direct costs of the product or service
Operating examples: materials, production labor or instructor wages, machinery use
Both: must be covered by the selling price
New location: overhead mostly new fixed cost, operating costs grow with customers
cards.example: Dance Frenzy's fourth studio would add overhead (rent, utilities, insurance, front desk) and operating costs (instructor wages, supplies); Jotter's overhead includes accounting staff and facility costs.

core: Absorption: fixed factory overhead in product cost
Variable: fixed overhead expensed in the period
detail: Absorption (full): required for external reports and taxes
Absorption unit cost: direct materials, direct labor, variable and fixed manufacturing overhead
Variable (direct): only variable manufacturing costs in the unit
Variable costing use: internal, shows contribution margin
Production > sales: absorption income higher
Why: some fixed overhead deferred in ending inventory
cards.formula: Absorption income minus Variable income = Fixed overhead per unit x (Units produced minus Units sold)
cards.example: Lumen Candle: absorption income $22,000 vs. variable $14,000; difference $8,000 = 2,000 unsold candles x $4 fixed overhead each.
cards.say_it: Absorption costing made profit $8,000 higher only because we built 2,000 extra candles, not because we sold more, so I would base the bonus on variable costing income.

detail: Avoidable: exist only because of a product or segment
Avoidable examples: supervisor or equipment lease only for that product, traceable advertising
Unavoidable examples: allocated factory rent, headquarters salaries
Stopping the product: just reassigns unavoidable costs to other products
Relevant: only avoidable costs in make or buy and keep or drop

cards.say_it: The VP's $60,000 saving counts $50,000 of rent and depreciation that will not go away; they just move to other products, so the true saving is $10,000.

core: Direct: traced to one product or department

Indirect (manufacturing overhead): factory rent, supervisor salaries, utilities, setups, inspections
Indirect assigned: using an allocation base
Depends on cost object: store manager's salary direct to store, indirect to each product

cards.formula: Prime cost = Direct materials + Direct labor
cards.example: Precision Machining: direct materials $25 and direct labor $20 per valve (prime cost $45); setups and inspections are indirect overhead allocated to each valve.
cards.say_it: Materials and labor can be traced to each valve, but setups are shared, so how we allocate them changes the reported cost of each product.

core: Keep if segment margin is positive
detail: Step 1: contribution margin = sales minus variable costs
Step 2: minus traceable fixed costs = segment margin
Step 3: ignore allocated common costs, they stay and shift to other segments
Step 4: positive margin dropped = company profit falls by it (plus lost linked sales)
Step 5: ways to improve it; qualitative factors like linked purchases, morale
cards.example: FitTech Smart Shoes: $300,000 minus $200,000 = $100,000 contribution margin, minus $60,000 traceable = $40,000 segment margin. It shows a $25,000 net loss only after a $65,000 common cost allocation, so dropping it would lower company profit by $40,000.
cards.say_it: Smart Shoes looks like a loser only because of the $65,000 allocation; it actually adds $40,000 to company profit, so we should keep it and improve it.

core: Relevant cost to make: variable + avoidable fixed
detail: Cost to make: variable + avoidable fixed + opportunity cost of space or capacity
Left out: unavoidable allocated costs, sunk costs
Buy cheaper: operating income rises by difference x units
Qualitative: supplier reliability, quality control, protecting designs
Also: how hard to restart production later
Thin margin: small price changes can reverse the decision

cards.say_it: Buying saves $10,000 a year, but if the supplier raises the price to $36, making is cheaper again, so I would negotiate a fixed price for several years.

detail: Financial exchange: any way value moves from buyer to seller
Cash and debit cards: money moves right away from what you already have
Checks: written orders telling a bank to pay
Credit cards and trade credit: pay later, which creates a debt
EFT: ACH, direct deposit, wire transfers move money between bank accounts, no paper

core: Pay on time (or early for a discount)
detail: Three-way match: invoice vs purchase order vs receiving record
Goal: pay only for what was ordered and received
Schedule by due date: avoids late fees, protects credit
Early payment discounts: take them when cheaper than borrowing
Pay by: check, EFT or autopay; keep the paid invoice
Entry: debit Accounts Payable, credit Cash
Paying late: hurts supplier relationships and credit ratings
Paying too early: gives up cash you could use
cards.example: Office Supplies Company receives a $500 web hosting invoice in October (debit Expense, credit Accounts Payable) and pays it November 15 (debit Accounts Payable $500, credit Cash $500).
cards.say_it: Our accounts payable process pays only verified invoices, on their due dates, so we keep our cash as long as possible without hurting our credit.
mistakes: Paying from a statement or phone call without checking the purchase order and receiving report

core: Credit unions: nonprofit co-ops, owned by members
detail: Both: checking, savings, loans, cards

Credit unions: membership by employer, location or group

Credit union downside: may have fewer business services

core: Debit: spends money you already have
Credit: borrows money you must repay
detail: Debit card: pulls straight from checking, no bill, no interest
Debit fraud risk: money leaves your account until the bank fixes it
Credit card: revolving loan with a monthly bill
Interest: charged if full balance not paid by due date, often 20% a year or more
Credit card upside: builds credit history, stronger fraud protection
Credit card downside: used carelessly, creates expensive debt
cards.example: Spending $500 on a debit card lowers your checking balance by $500 today. Spending $500 on a credit card at 24% APR and paying only interest costs about $10 a month ($500 x 24% / 12) while the $500 still remains owed.
cards.say_it: I recommend a business credit card for small purchases only if the balance is paid in full each month, so we get the record keeping and fraud protection without paying interest.
mistakes: Thinking a credit card payment is "spending your own money": it is borrowing until the bill is paid

core: Each dollar buys less over time

detail: Measured by: Consumer Price Index (CPI)

Business: material and wage costs rise, update budgets and prices

cards.formula: Real interest rate is about Nominal rate minus Inflation rate
cards.example: A savings account paying 2% during 3% inflation has a real return of about minus 1%: the balance grows but buys less.
cards.say_it: Our cash reserve should earn at least the inflation rate, otherwise it quietly loses value even though the balance never goes down.

core: Interest earned on loans and investments

detail: Bank's main source of earnings

Cause: fixed-rate loans while deposits reprice with the market
Interest rate risk: that mismatch

cards.formula: Net interest income = Interest earned minus Interest paid

cards.say_it: Our loans are locked at fixed rates while our deposit costs move with the market, so a rate increase could cut net interest income by 42%.

core: Operating income − minimum required return on assets used
detail: Measures: dollars earned above the hurdle rate

cards.say_it: The jacket line earns $32,000 more than our 12% minimum, so on residual income it is clearly a good project even though it pulls the division's ROI down.

detail: Use: compare divisions of different sizes

core: Seller minimum: variable cost + lost contribution margin
detail: Lost contribution margin: opportunity cost of outside sales given up
Idle capacity: no lost sales, minimum = variable cost
Subtract costs avoided on internal sales (e.g. selling commissions)
Buyer won't pay more than an outside supplier charges
Price in between: both divisions better off
Minimum above maximum: company better off buying outside
cards.formula: Minimum = Variable cost per unit + Lost contribution margin per unit; Maximum = Outside market price
cards.example: Northwind with idle capacity: minimum $8 (the $1 selling cost is avoided internally), maximum $13. A negotiated $10.50 gives Fabric 20,000 x 2.50 = $50,000 more and saves Apparel $50,000. At full capacity: minimum = 8 + lost margin 5 = $13, so the company is indifferent.
cards.say_it: Since Fabric has idle capacity, any price from $8 to $13 works; $14 is outside the range and would push Apparel to buy outside, costing the company $100,000.
mistakes: Including fixed costs in the minimum or ignoring whether the seller has idle capacity

core: Transfers risk of a large loss to an insurer

core: Rate variance: wage different from standard
Efficiency variance: more or fewer hours than allowed
detail: Rate causes: overtime, higher paid workers, raises
Efficiency causes: training, scheduling, machine problems, poor materials
Standard hours allowed = actual output x standard hours per unit
Owner of both: production supervisor
Together: total labor variance, often the largest cost problem in a case
cards.formula: Rate variance = (Actual rate minus Standard rate) x Actual hours; Efficiency variance = (Actual hours minus Standard hours allowed) x Standard rate
cards.example: Crumb & Co.: rate ($16 minus $15) x 1,300 hours = $1,300 U; efficiency (1,300 minus 1,200) x $15 = $1,500 U; total labor $2,800 U.
cards.say_it: Labor is our biggest problem: 100 extra hours at a dollar more per hour, so let's look at overtime, new hires and scheduling.

core: Price variance: paying more or less than standard
Quantity variance: using more or less than allowed
detail: Price variance owner: purchasing manager
Quantity variance owner: production
Standard quantity allowed = actual output x standard quantity per unit
Trade-off: cheap materials (favorable price) can waste more (unfavorable quantity)
Read the two together
Total materials variance = actual cost − standard cost allowed
cards.formula: Price variance = (Actual price minus Standard price) x Actual quantity; Quantity variance = (Actual quantity minus Standard quantity allowed) x Standard price
cards.example: Crumb & Co. flour: price ($0.48 minus $0.50) x 25,000 lbs = $500 F; quantity (25,000 minus 24,000) x $0.50 = $500 U; net $0.

cards.say_it: The extra 2,000 loaves earned us $6,000, but we gave back $6,600 through lower prices and higher costs, so operations are not fine.

core: GAAP: probable + estimable → accrue (minimum of range)
IFRS: more likely than not → provision (midpoint of range)
detail: GAAP (ASC 450) probable: likely to occur, reasonably estimable → accrued
GAAP reasonably possible: disclosed in the notes
GAAP remote: ignored
GAAP range: no amount more likely, so accrue the minimum
IFRS (IAS 37): provision when outflow probable (more likely than not), so it can accrue sooner
IFRS range: midpoint when all outcomes equally likely
Both: note disclosure of significant contingencies
cards.example: A lawsuit loss estimated between $30,000 and $50,000 with no best estimate is accrued at $30,000 under GAAP and $40,000 under IFRS.
cards.say_it: Accruing a probable loss is not admitting guilt; it simply keeps the statements from misleading lenders and investors.

core: Could change a reasonable user's decision
detail: Depends on: size and nature
Immaterial items: simpler treatment allowed (expense a $20 stapler)
Material items: must follow GAAP and be disclosed
Auditors: set materiality as a percentage of a benchmark (pre-tax income, total revenue, assets)
Performance materiality: lower amount used to plan testing
Material by nature: small items such as fraud by an executive
cards.formula: Example benchmark: materiality = 5% x pre-tax income; performance materiality = about 50% to 75% of materiality
cards.example: With pre-tax income of $600,000, 5% materiality is $30,000 and 75% performance materiality is $22,500, so $15,000 of errors is not material but should still be corrected.
cards.say_it: An error is material when it is big enough, or serious enough, to change what a banker or investor would decide.
mistakes: Thinking immaterial errors can be ignored; they should still be corrected and tracked

cards.term: Research and development costs: GAAP vs IFRS
core: GAAP: expense all R&D as incurred
IFRS: expense research, capitalize development (criteria met)
detail: GAAP (ASC 730): R&D expensed, future benefits uncertain; software has special rules
IFRS (IAS 38): research expensed; development capitalized as an intangible asset
IFRS criteria: technical feasibility, intent and ability to complete and use or sell
More criteria: probable future benefits, resources to finish, reliable measurement
Amortization: starts once the asset is available for use
Effect: IFRS shows higher income and assets in the year of spending
cards.formula: IFRS income advantage this year = capitalized development costs
cards.example: Of $1,000,000 R&D, IFRS expenses $400,000 research and capitalizes $600,000 development; GAAP expenses all $1,000,000, so IFRS income and assets are $600,000 higher.
cards.say_it: Capitalizing is not fake profit; IFRS records proven development as an asset and expenses it later through amortization.

core: U.S. GAAP: rules based, detailed guidance
IFRS: principles based, relies on judgment
detail: GAAP: specific rules, bright lines, industry guidance
GAAP pros: consistency, easier to audit
GAAP con: can encourage structuring transactions to fit the rule
IFRS: broad principles, professional judgment to show economic substance
IFRS pro: fits unusual situations; con: more variation between companies
Reality: both use principles and rules; difference of degree
cards.example: IFRS lets Novus judge when development work has become a valuable asset, while GAAP simply says expense all R&D.
cards.say_it: GAAP tends to give you the exact rule, while IFRS gives you the principle and trusts your judgment.

core: Divisible by 2: amount on the wrong side
detail: First: find the exact difference
Half test: half of difference = an actual amount, so item added instead of subtracted (debited vs credited)
Divide by 9: two digits swapped (transposition, 54 written as 45) or decimal slid (slide error)
Otherwise: look for an omitted item equal to the difference
Payoff: turns a frustrating search into a targeted check
cards.formula: Difference / 2 = amount entered on the wrong side; Difference divisible by 9 = transposition or slide error
cards.example: The book side is $10 too high; $10 / 2 = $5, the exact interest amount the intern subtracted instead of added.
cards.say_it: Because the difference was exactly twice the $5 interest, I knew right away the item was on the wrong side.
